claims.claim: Remedy recount under a stated coding rule. Rule: count a statement only when he links it to nerves, fear, pressure or readiness for a big test AND names what settled or settles it; exclude pure craft (accents, tennis, notebooks, emotional-access rituals) unless he ties it to nerves; count each source once per category; exclude unverified speakers; statements of nerves with no mechanism ('I'll be fine', 'I got over that quickly') are not remedies. Tally: tuning out or narrowing 3 (S01 C63; S04 C70/C32; S30 C128), 4 if S49 C203 ('day by day', about acclaim) is admitted; structure arranged in advance 2 (S02 C14 prep mode; S20 C135/C136 rehearsals); security from a vetted team 1 (S48 C191 'safe hands'); competent others make it easier 2 (S48, S49 C194); familiarity or meeting people 2 (S02 C14/C66; S54 C212); company against rumination 1 (S03 C68); results 2 (S20 C134; S50 C204); effort-then-release rule 1 (S47 C196); self-talk reframe 1 (S04 C76). So: Six-leaning (structure plus vetted team) 3; Nine-leaning (tuning out) 3 to 4; shared Six/Nine (others' competence, familiarity, company) 5; Three-leaning (results) 2.
claims.inference: Supportable wording: 'When he says what settled his nerves, he most often names other people (their competence, or getting to know them), which fits a Six or a Nine; structure arranged in advance and tuning out appear about equally often; results appear twice.' The previous wording ('more often describe structure arranged in advance than pressure muted', verify-01) is not supported and is withdrawn. Changes from the research brief's tally: Close's line (C19) is excluded because in context it is gratitude, not about nerves (S10 recheck); the MovieZine 'preparation and rituals' answer (C210) is excluded because in context it is a technique for reaching emotion, and 'release stress' is not in the audio; C135 and C136 count once because they come from one source; and C204 is added as a second result-shaped resolution, which the brief missed. Probable but excluded pending visual speaker checks: S61 C220 ('best team in the world backing [us]') would add 1 to the vetted-team category; S62 C213 (reception-based 'ease') would add 1 to results. Readings: against Three, people and structure (8) clearly outnumber results (2). Against Nine, the remedy record does not separate the types. So Six over Nine cannot rest on remedy, and must rest, if anywhere, on the intensity and self-push items (C195, C200, C205, C209, C172).
claims.alternative: The categories are judgment calls. 'Competent others make it easier' could be coded Six (reliance) rather than shared, which would make Six-leaning 5 against Nine-leaning 3 to 4. Equally, 'safe hands' and the rehearsals could be coded as idiom and routine, which leaves almost nothing Six-specific. Both codings are recorded so a reviewer can redo the count.

claims.claim: Interpretation: his clearest break from a default path is the self-set challenge to play young Haymitch as the opposite of Harrelson's character after two months of study, which the novel licensed but he chose.

claims.inference: Per enneagram-06 the steering paragraph now rests first on C125 (S30) with the novel's licence noted (C163). The smaller items ('I'm leaving', the self-set deadline) follow with the concession that none cost him much. The music request and the empty-slate item were cut for length.
claims.alternative: Departing from a predecessor is standard craft, and the novel's arc makes the choice obvious.

claims.claim: By THR's account, as a teenager he skipped classes to pursue auditions and small roles.
claims.passage: a teenager who skipped class to chase auditions
claims.inference: S30: 'Zada continued blowing off classes as he pursued auditions and small roles in Aussie TV projects like The Speedway Murders and Total Control.' Added to the Type 3 record per critic-04 as early appetite the record supports.
claims.alternative: Hating school ('I hated, hated school', S30) explains the truancy as well as appetite does.

claims.claim: He told Flaunt in 2025 that he constantly reminds himself he is still learning and not to be afraid of whether his work is good.
claims.passage: reminding himself in 2025 "not to be afraid of whether it's good or not"
claims.inference: S04: 'I'm just constantly reminding myself that I'm still learning and not to be afraid of whether it's good or not.' Restored per critic-04 as a dated failure fear.
claims.alternative: A stock newcomer line; also a coping move that de-emphasises results.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the fears he names, from 'embarrass myself' at 14 to 'deathly nervous' about idols in 2026, concern being judged or doing badly, which on the article's key leans Three.
claims.passage: So do his fears.
claims.inference: The count requested by critic-04 and enneagram-01: C117 (S30, age 14), C134 (S20, February 2025), C13 (S02, July 2025), C76 (S04, 2025), C175 (S01, June 2026). None concerns losing support or footing. The type answer (C50) and FAQ 1 state this. Research (2026-10-04, second refresh): Additions to the count, all evaluative or about exposure: 'quite insecure... expressing myself' (C206, S45), public-speaking nerves at the GQ awards (C215, S58), and first-day fear on the Sunrise set (C217, S59). None concerns losing support or footing.
claims.alternative: A Six can fear failing too; fear content is not decisive on its own.

claims.passage: This reading accounts for the manner of his pursuit, tracking the competition quietly and preparing with other people. It does not fully explain the appetite Lind saw, and that tension stays open.

claims.claim: Orientation: Invisible Boys (Stan, 2025) was filmed in Perth and Geraldton in early 2024; We Were Liars (Prime Video, 2025) in Nova Scotia later in 2024; East of Eden (Netflix, 2026) in New Zealand from October 2024 to March 2025; Sunrise on the Reaping in Spain and Germany from July to November 2025, with Glenn Close and Ralph Fiennes in the cast.
claims.passage: The four projects, in the order he shot them: _Invisible Boys_ (Stan, 2025), a series lead filmed in Perth and Geraldton in early 2024; _We Were Liars_ (Prime Video, 2025), a series lead filmed in Nova Scotia later that year; _East of Eden_ (Netflix, 2026), a two-episode part in a series which filmed in New Zealand from October 2024 to March 2025 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_Eden_(2026_miniseries))); and _Sunrise on the Reaping_ (Lionsgate film, 2026), with Zada as Haymitch, shot in Spain and Germany from July to November 2025 alongside Glenn Close and Ralph Fiennes.
claims.inference: Added per unfamiliar-02. S23/S25: Invisible Boys filming in Perth and Geraldton in early 2024; S30: 'It was while shooting the first season of Liars, in 2024' and 'flew to Nova Scotia'; S02 places nights in Halifax; S16: New Zealand, October 2024 to March 2025; S21: principal photography July to November 28, 2025, in Spain and Germany, with Close and Fiennes in the cast, and the November 20, 2026 release; S22: Lionsgate's casting announcement of Zada as Haymitch. S03 gives his own order ('Invisible Boys... straight to We Were Liars... straight to East of Eden... straight to Hunger Games').
claims.alternative: Production windows are approximate where sources give months rather than dates.

claims.claim: Interpretation: few of his choices cost him much, so the reading rests mostly on statements repeated across years and interviewers, which keeps confidence at medium.
claims.passage: Few of his choices cost him much, so this reading rests mostly on statements that repeat across years and interviewers, which keeps confidence at medium.
claims.inference: Per critic-05: the school exit cost little at home (C120), the flight home has a production explanation (C107), and the family trip a pay-cheque one. The earlier promise to lean 'on what he did, especially when it cost him something' is withdrawn because the article could not keep it. Research (2026-10-04, second refresh): Confidence is now low, not medium (C225, C226). The passage must change.

claims.passage: What settles those nerves is the case for Enneagram Type 6, which in this nine-type model of core motivation is the type organized around security and around who can be relied on.

Research (2026-10-04, second refresh): The thesis framing ('what settles those nerves is the case for Type 6') overstates the case after C171's recount. A future draft would need to present Six as a low-confidence lead with Three as a live second reading.

Research (2026-10-04, second refresh): Pre-release data points: C202 (effort over applause) and C204 (nerves answered by the finished film's quality). Neither settles the test.

claims.review_trigger: After November 20, 2026 and after early 2027: record whether he moved, how he describes what steadies him, and whether he defers big decisions; revise this paragraph and C82 accordingly.

claims.claim: Interpretation: nervousness, gratitude and found-family language are the house style of promotional interviews and would appear whatever his type.
claims.passage: Nervousness, gratitude and "the cast became a family" are the house style of those formats, and a newcomer sharing a cast list with Glenn Close and Ralph Fiennes would produce them whatever his type.
claims.inference: The quoted phrase is the article's paraphrase of a press cliche, not a quotation from him, though he uses the idea (S01: 'this is a perfectly curated team. It's also a family'; S05: 'I felt like I was already part of a family'). Protected by four reviewers; kept verbatim. S21 supplies the Close/Fiennes cast list.
claims.alternative: None; a statement of the source base's confound.

claims.claim: In June 2025 he said the Sunrise audition put him 'through the wringer', that he was glad because he learned so much, and 'Now I'm just so excited to know that I'm going to be in safe hands.' In October 2026 he called the same process 'what felt like an unnecessary hell' that he came to see as necessary.
claims.inference: S48 (June 18, 2025): 'It's a very big, important character, and they needed to get it right. So obviously, they put me through the wringer a bit... But I'm glad they did because I learned so much in that period of time. Now I'm just so excited to know that I'm going to be in safe hands.' S47 (October 2, 2026): 'They put me through what felt like an unnecessary hell until I got there and I was shooting... And then you understand that it is necessary to put someone through a long and hard process because that's what the film is.' S54/S19 (June 11, 2025) gives the same audition a familiarity rationale (C213). This is the clearest security-shaped remedy in his own words: a demanding vetting reassures him that the team is competent. It is reassurance from a vetted team, not from his own result and not from ease. Coded 'vetted-team security' in C171.
claims.alternative: 'In safe hands' is a stock idiom of franchise press, used of fans' expectations as often as of actors' nerves, and it is said in a release-week profile. It may express pleasure at a competent production (a Nine's or Three's reading would be equally comfortable) rather than relief from a security fear. It is one phrase in one interview.

claims.claim: In June 2025 he said that since the Hunger Games announcement he has had to be 'a lot more careful about what I'm doing and saying, which is always a good thing. But it's a little scary sometimes,' having 'never really expected to get much attention'.
claims.inference: S48: 'As long as I was acting, I was happy and I never really expected to get much attention for it. But I feel like my life kind of changed with [the Hunger Games] announcement. It's a different world now. I've got to be a lot more careful about what I'm doing and saying, which is always a good thing. But it's a little scary sometimes.' He welcomes vigilance ('always a good thing') while naming it as frightening. Six-flavoured: caution under exposure is endorsed, not resented. Listed with C193 and C197 among the Six-specific markers the record lacked (C224).
claims.alternative: Every newly famous young actor is media-trained to be careful, and this is what publicists tell them to say. 'Careful about what I'm saying' is equally image management (Three). The line does not show worst-case scanning in practice.

claims.claim: He kept to Zoe Kazan's emailed instruction not to watch the 1955 film through the East of Eden shoot, saying 'I was so tempted throughout the entire shoot, but I felt like it was a bad omen'; he says Kazan's reason was that his first tape, made without seeing the film, showed his own take.
claims.inference: S48 (June 2025): 'After his first callback audition, "I had an email specifically from Zoe saying, 'Do not watch the movie.' I was so tempted throughout the entire shoot, but I felt like it was a bad omen."' S49 and S50 (September 30, 2026) give Kazan's reason as he understood it: 'I had sent in an audition without seeing it first and... she liked my personality, my take on the character.' S57: Kazan says 'he did not audition with a James Dean impression'. This extends C22 and C95. He framed breaking a trusted authority's rule as a bad omen and kept to it against his own temptation. That is compliance with a chosen authority reinforced by superstition, a Six-flavoured pattern.
claims.alternative: The instruction served his own creative interest, since Kazan wanted his take, so compliance cost little. Actors often avoid a predecessor's performance. 'Bad omen' may be a light, superstitious turn of phrase common among actors rather than anxious vigilance. A deferring Nine complies just as readily.

claims.claim: Twice, fifteen months apart, he described fear of acting opposite admired co-stars resolving through their competence: 'As much as acting with someone like Florence or Chris is terrifying, it's also so easy because they're so good at what they're doing that you just don't have to work as hard' (June 2025) and 'I was so nervous to begin with, but it makes your work so much easier. You end up going to work with people that are working so hard' (September 30, 2026).
claims.inference: S48 paragraph 13 (June 18, 2025) and S49 at 01:41-01:59 (September 30, 2026), both about the East of Eden cast (Pugh, Abbott, Anders). The pattern repeats across interviewers and 15 months: fear of admired people (C13, C93) settles once their competence carries the work. Coded 'competent others make it easier' in C171, a category shared by Six (reliance on capable others) and Nine (relief at reduced effort).
claims.alternative: 'Great actors make it easier' is a standard junket compliment. The wording stresses reduced effort ('you just don't have to work as hard', 'so much easier'), which fits a Nine's relief at ease as well as a Six's reliance. It does not separate them.

claims.claim: Describing Johnny in We Were Liars, he said: 'I'm a little more reserved, but it was really fun to just force myself out of my comfort zone.'
claims.inference: S48 paragraph 12. Self-push against comfort, offered as enjoyable. Together with C201, C206 and C211 this is the new evidence against a comfort-seeking Nine.
claims.alternative: It is about playing a character, and 'out of my comfort zone' is a cliché of actor interviews. Pushing past comfort for a role is craft, not proof of a non-Nine motive.

claims.claim: He describes a motto 'ingrained in me by my dad' for handling pressure: 'You work as hard as you can, and then you let it go because there's nothing else that you can worry about.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraph 4 (October 2, 2026), introduced by the writer's 'The pressure might wear on another actor, but Zada carries the weight of such company lightly.' He names a trusted authority as the source of a worry-management rule. Effort first, then release. It mirrors C137 (absorb everything, then let go). Coded 'mixed: effort then release' in C171.
claims.alternative: It is a generic work ethic. 'Let it go' fits a Nine's release, 'work as hard as you can' fits a Three's effort, and the authority-derived rule fits a Six. It discriminates nothing on its own. The writer's 'carries the weight lightly' is her framing.

claims.claim: Asked whether he feels the pressure of inheriting Haymitch, he said: 'I don't know if this is a dangerous thing to say, but I don't really care... I don't want to create for someone else's opinion. I want to create something that I feel and then hope that people feel with me.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraph 14 (October 2, 2026). This explicitly rejects approval as the aim, which counts against an approval-driven Three, and it echoes 'my own shoes' (C126). 'I don't know if this is a dangerous thing to say' flags awareness of risk in speaking (cf. C192). Coded 'rejects evaluation as the settler' in C171.
claims.alternative: Saying you create for yourself is the expected artist's answer in a magazine profile. It sits against his repeated fear of how admired people perceive him (C13, C93, C175), so as a self-description it is aspiration as much as report. 'Something that I feel' is Four-compatible.

claims.claim: He says that under audition pressure for Haymitch he did an impression of Harrelson: 'I moved myself into an impression, hoping that that was what was going to push me over the line in terms of securing the role,' until, per Vanity Fair, Francis Lawrence encouraged him to find his own voice; on September 30, 2026 he said he began with 'a perfect impersonation of Woody... And then from there was dialing it back and bringing my own.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraphs 11-12 place the impression in the audition ('Harrelson's ghost very nearly cost Zada the part'). The Lawrence note is the writer's paraphrase. S50 (00:35-01:06) is about the accent: start with the impression, then dial it back. S30 places a two-month Harrelson study 'after he signed for the part' and the opposite-of-Woody challenge at the start of shooting (C125). The accounts can be combined (impression in the audition, deeper study after signing, departure on set), but the record does not establish the order exactly. This is the record's clearest act of shaping himself to what he thought would win, a Three datum (C225). It weakens the claim that he never performs to win (C157).
claims.alternative: A Six reading also fits: under uncertainty he leaned on the proven template, then took the director's correction from a trusted authority. Imitating a predecessor's accent is also ordinary early-stage craft. Kazan's testimony (S57) that he did not do a Dean impression for Cal shows the impression was not his only strategy.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair observed in October 2026 that he is 'a resistant poster' whose Instagram 'has less than two dozen photos spread out over three years', mostly promotional, and he said: 'I have a real problem with phones. My honest opinion is that it's an epidemic.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraphs 22-23. An observable public choice: he forgoes personal visibility during a breakout year, for a stated values reason. Mild evidence against an image-driven Three. It is not evidence for Six.
claims.alternative: Low posting is common among actors and can be a rep-advised mystique strategy. The account exists and is used for promotion. The writer notes he is 'channeling Harrelson', who has no phone. No cost to his career is shown, so this is not a demonstrated costly choice.
claims.review_trigger: At the next refresh, check whether his posting pattern has changed after the November 2026 release before repeating the observation; date it 'as of October 2026'.

claims.claim: He describes his own appetite and self-regard in Vanity Fair: as a teenager 'I became really hungry and obsessive about trying to just better my craft'; 'I feel like most actors are lying that they don't watch themselves... We are some of the most vain creatures on the planet'; 'Sometimes I feel like I'm more of a fan than an artist.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraphs 16, 25-26. 'Hungry and obsessive' adds to the appetite collaborators describe (C26, C131) and to C174. Enjoying watching himself is Three-compatible. 'Hungry and obsessive' also resists a Nine's inertia.
claims.alternative: 'Most vain creatures' is a wry generalisation about actors in a profile, not a confession. 'Better my craft' is about skill, which fits any type. The fan line points toward enthusiasm, not image.

claims.claim: Woody Harrelson told Vanity Fair: 'He's about to be a big star, and I think he's got his head on his shoulders. He's going to be tough enough to deal with all that comes with stardom.' On TODAY on September 30, 2026, Harrelson's recorded message warned: 'it's okay when people tell you you're great. The big problem is when you start believing [it].'
claims.inference: Named third-party testimony, the only kind the last verifier would accept. It does not meet that test. It predicts how he will handle stardom; it does not describe how he handled a pressured moment. Harrelson had met him once, after filming (S47, S30, S60), and says on TODAY that he has not seen the performance. It does not separate Six, Three or Nine.
claims.alternative: Courtesy praise from a predecessor in two promotional settings.

claims.claim: Replying on TODAY (September 30, 2026) to Harrelson's warning, he said: 'It's lovely advice and it's true. I think for me, it's just about the work really... all the applause. It's really nice, but I feel like my happiness comes from just working really hard and putting my best foot forward all the time.'
claims.inference: S49 at 02:45-03:07, recorded before the November 20, 2026 Sunrise release, which tests C82 and C183 in advance. He names effort, not acclaim, as the source of his happiness. Coded 'rejects acclaim as the settler' in C171. It does not count as a November press-cycle statement.
claims.alternative: It is the socially expected reply to a mentor's televised warning. 'Putting my best foot forward' is itself performance-framed, and a Three can sincerely identify with hard work. A self-report of not caring about applause is weak evidence about whether applause steadies him.

claims.claim: Asked on TODAY whether he could 'step back and just soak this all in' after Variety's actors-to-watch list, he said: 'Not really. I'm not trying to. I just want to... do day by day, you know, just get through, get through today.'
claims.inference: S49 at 03:07-03:22. Narrowing focus to the day in front of him, about acclaim rather than nerves. Coded 'tuning out or narrowing' in C171 under the loose rule only, because it answers a question about acclaim, not nerves.
claims.alternative: It was a premiere-day morning-show answer on a busy day. 'Day by day' is a cliché that fits a Six (managing the next step), a Nine (not taking it in) or simple fatigue.

claims.claim: On September 30, 2026, asked about the Sunrise release, he said: 'I'm so nervous for it to come out but I saw it recently and it is fantastic. It is such a special movie and the performances are out of this world. Every department is just working, firing on all cylinders.'
claims.inference: S50 at 00:06-00:21. Nerves about the release are answered by the quality of the finished film. That is a result-shaped settler, the second in the record after C134 ('terrified I'd be dreadful! But I think it's come out all right'). He credits the result to 'every department', so it is a collective result, not a personal one. Coded 'results' in C171. It weakens 'the fix is rarely a result' (C166, C157).
claims.alternative: Promotional enthusiasm for an unreleased film is obligatory, and the 'nervous... but it's great' formula is junket idiom. Because he credits the whole team, a Six reading (reassurance from a competent collective) is also available.

claims.claim: Contrasting himself with Florence Pugh on the East of Eden set, he said: 'I'm intense you know I walk around in circles and I keep very much to myself and I play music', while she was 'laughing and playing with the crew'; before one long scene he listened to West End Girls on a loop 'for like seven hours'; he called Cal 'a dark space to stay in for a while but I'm really glad that I did because I'm so happy with the result.'
claims.inference: S50 at 02:53-03:51 and 03:55-04:17. Solitary absorption and a self-run ritual on set, with the cost justified by the result. It resists a Nine who merges with the room or seeks ease. It also fits his repeated pattern of immersion followed by release (C137).
claims.alternative: This is method-style immersion, which 9takes's own Austin Butler profile (S44) treats as compatible with Type 9 ('disappearing into roles'). Keeping to oneself also fits the Nine's withdrawn stance and a Four's or Five's absorption. 'So happy with the result' is Three-compatible. It does not separate cleanly.

claims.claim: In a November 2025 Casting Guild interview recorded during the Sunrise shoot, he said his father 'literally forc[ed]' him into a Romeo and Juliet production at about 15 ('no, it's cringe, don't make me go'), that he 'was quite insecure I think in that space and expressing myself that way', and that coming off stage he 'got the bug for it'.
claims.inference: S45 at 01:06-02:55: he played Benvolio and the Apothecary in five scenes; theatre was 'putting myself in a more vulnerable place... being in front of like 200 person crowd'. S48 (June 2025): 'I'm not acting. Acting's cringe.' S30 dates the production to age 14 and says his father made it a condition of his skipping school (C151); S45 says about 15. Do not fix the age; '14 or 15' or 'as a teenager' is supported. The resistance was insecurity about self-exposure, overcome by a trusted authority's push. This adds to C117 ('embarrass myself').
claims.alternative: Ordinary teenage self-consciousness. Being pushed by a parent says more about the parent than about his motive. The resistance and the passivity until pushed fit a Nine as well (C174).

claims.claim: In the Casting Guild interview he named as his most valuable lesson that actors like Hugo Weaving and Ryan Gosling are 'lovely to everyone on set', 'try their best to remember everyone's names', and that this 'should come first before anything else... to try and make the environment as nice as possible.'
claims.inference: S45 at 04:34-05:43. A relational-harmony value stated in the least promotional setting in the record. He adds that actors on sets are often 'left alone'.
claims.alternative: Kindness to crew is a stock actorly virtue. The value fits Nine (harmony), Two (helping) and Six (belonging) equally and does not discriminate.

claims.claim: In the Casting Guild interview he said he has no fixed method ('I don't really have like a method... It's evolved so much since Invisible Boys, because I'm trying to finding my footing as I'm going'), described daily tennis for a month or more before We Were Liars, and said 'I'm very big with my accents... I stay in the accent all day on set. And I work them meticulously beforehand.'
claims.inference: S45 at 10:32-12:13. Extensive advance preparation, with a provisional method that confirms C21 and C138 in a non-promotional setting. S47 adds notebooks 'full of symbols and codes that correlated with specific book pages' and wandering casinos at midnight in Cal's costume ('It sounds insane, but it worked so well'). Under C171's rule these are craft preparation, not linked to nerves, so they are excluded from the remedy tally.
claims.alternative: Thorough preparation is taught craft and the norm for leads in big productions.

claims.claim: In the Casting Guild interview he said: 'I can't sidestep these things... I have to be a hundred percent there every single day to play that character truthfully and... it all pays off', and of audience impact: 'I don't know if I, I really do it for that. Honestly, I do really do it because I just love acting.' He described the reward of acting as a feeling, when preparation, scene partners and environment are right, of 'everything... vibrating at the right level', which 'I'm trying to chase the whole time'.
claims.inference: S45 at 05:56-06:53, 13:33-14:03 and 14:40-14:53. A duty-and-commitment frame and an absorbed-flow reward, with impact and approval disclaimed as motive, in a setting with no release attached. It counts against a Three and against an inert Nine, and it fits C205.
claims.alternative: These are generic actor answers to generic questions. Disclaiming approval is expected. Flow-seeking fits most types.

claims.claim: Asked in June 2025 what he would take from We Were Liars into the Hunger Games, he said 'preparation and rituals': experimenting with 'different ways to come into scenes', 'music and meditation and stretching', the stretching being a way 'to get to an emotional place' for emotional scenes, while 'I'm still very young into this and I'm still learning'.
claims.inference: S51 at 04:03-04:54 (the question is addressed to Joseph; S52 is the same answer in a clip titled for him alone). In context the rituals are techniques for reaching emotion in big scenes, not for managing nerves, so C171's strict rule excludes them from the remedy tally. The research brief's 'you can release stress' is not confirmed (two Whisper models hear 'you really stress').
claims.alternative: Ordinary craft experimentation.

claims.claim: Asked in October 2026 who encouraged him early on, he named his older brother Hal, with whom he auditioned 'every day together' for about four years through COVID and the strikes ('his encouragement was just like just everything to me'), his parents, and his acting coach Miranda Harcourt, who 'taught me everything that I know and introduced me to my manager'.
claims.inference: S53 at 03:32-04:43. This corroborates C05, C06 and C186 (preparing with Hal) and adds a coach he credits for his guidance. He gives others, not himself, the credit for his start, which fits S47's 'helping hands' frame and S56's account of advocates (C214). The answer at 04:43-05:55 ('considered an equal', 'true belief in me') is Joe Anders's and must not be attributed to Zada.
claims.alternative: The question asked who encouraged him, so the gratitude was elicited. Crediting mentors is universal in junkets. 'Four years' and 'hundreds of takes' are loose figures.

claims.claim: On the Swooon video (June 11, 2025) he said the Sunrise audition process mattered 'not just to learn about the character, but to meet all the people I was working with and feel comfortable. And I'm comfortable and I'm excited and I'm nervous'.
claims.inference: S54 at 00:35-01:00, which resolves the old S19/S12 wording task. 'Meet all the people... and feel comfortable' is the reading of Whisper large-v3-turbo, CinemaBlend (S12) and Swooon's text (S19). Whisper small.en hears 'make all the people I was working with feel comfortable', so a small residual doubt remains. Coded 'familiarity' in C171, a category shared with Nine. 'I'm going to smash this' (research brief) is not used: it is uncertain in the audio, and S19's text gives 'You're going to smash it' to Esther McGregor.
claims.alternative: Meeting the team and feeling comfortable is ordinary and fits Nine's ease as well as Six's footing.

claims.claim: Asked in a two-person TV Fanatic interview (June 17, 2025) whether he felt pressure, a speaker who is probably Zada said the response to the casting was 'so lovely' that 'I struggled so hard to find a single bad' comment, that this gave 'that sense of just, you know, ease', and that 'now that it's finished and it's all about to come out, that pressure comes back in.' The following 'security kind of blanket... Emily, are you happy?... you just have to trust' passage is probably Esther McGregor's.
claims.inference: Speakers are inferred from voice pitch, not seen. Median F0 in 03:30-03:39 and 03:42-03:57 is 133-170 Hz, matching Zada's 99-165 Hz in S45 and S50. 03:39-03:42 ('Yeah, I was looking for it') and 03:57-04:31 are 200-246 Hz, matching McGregor's 229 Hz earlier in the same video. Not used in C171's tally until verified visually.

claims.claim: We Were Liars co-creator Julie Plec told Page Six in June 2025 that the crew 'would stop their work and stand and watch him act', and that Mamie Gummer, who plays his mother, called Zoe Kazan to say 'You have got to see this kid'; he told Vanity Fair in 2026 that luck and 'lucky stars' guide his career, a theme the writer says he 'frequently returns' to.
claims.inference: S56 paragraphs 2, 4-6, and S47 paragraphs 3 and 16 ('I got really lucky at 18'). Others advocated for him, and he credits luck and ancestors (C54) more than his own drive. This is the attribution pattern the research brief used against Three. The testimony concerns talent, not pressure.
claims.alternative: Gratitude and luck talk are a junket convention and a common modesty move for a fast-rising young actor. Plec relays others' texts in her own release week. Being championed by others is a fact about them.

claims.claim: Star Observer reported on April 4, 2026 that at the GQ Australia awards, where he was named Breakthrough Actor of the Year, 'a nervous Zada' apologised for 'his nervousness with public speaking', misspoke ('rooting me... uh, rooting for me') and 'tried to laugh it off'.
claims.inference: The only observed public instance of his nerves in the record, at an awards event with no release junket attached. It shows evaluation and exposure nerves (consistent with C173) handled by owning them and laughing.
claims.alternative: Public-speaking nerves at an award acceptance are near-universal and do not separate any types. The report is second-hand. IF (S46) dates the award to 2025, so the ceremony date is not fixed.

claims.claim: Accounts of his first exchange with Woody Harrelson after the Sunrise shoot differ: to EW (August 27, 2026) he said they 'spoke after shooting' and 'I asked him a bunch of questions'; to Entertainment Tonight (September 17, 2026) that 'we called and we spoke... I had so many questions for him... But he really wanted to hear about me'; to THR (October 1, 2026) that at a dinner party where he sat beside Harrelson, 'I couldn't think of any questions. I forgot everything I wanted to ask him.'
claims.inference: S60 (EW via Yahoo), S55 (Whisper 06:38-07:01) and S30 paragraph 'It was only after he'd shot Hunger Games'. S47 adds that Harrelson first congratulated him by text through his niece and that they 'were finally able to meet in person after Zada finished filming'. The phone call and the dinner may be different encounters, but none of the sources says so, and EW's 'asked him a bunch of questions' is hard to square with THR's blank if they are the same meeting. The baseline draft's hook (C127) presents the dinner blank as the first meeting without this tension.
claims.alternative: Retellings of a starstruck moment drift with each interviewer. The THR version may compress a call and a later dinner. Either way the event is ordinary (C152).

claims.claim: He told EW (August 2026) he was 's--- scared' filming the Cornucopia run on his first day of the Sunrise shoot: 'being ready to jump and having to wait for the countdown. And looking around and seeing all your competition around you and trying to keep you focused.'
claims.inference: First-day nerves on a vast set, handled by staying focused. It fits his pattern of nerves at the start of a job (C14, C65) and does not discriminate.
claims.alternative: The answer is shaped to the film's story (the countdown 'was very fitting'), and first-day fear is universal.

claims.claim: In October 2026 Vanity Fair reported he hopes 'to put down roots somewhere, maybe LA or New York', and that he is writing a dramedy with his brother, 'possibly with an eye toward directing it someday': 'It might be a piece of shit... It probably is. But we'll make it work.'
claims.inference: S47 paragraph 27. This updates C40 (the move: S47 names LA or New York, S30 names L.A. in early 2027) and C167 (the co-written film with Hal is still in progress as of October 2026, now described as a dramedy). The self-deprecating 'piece of shit' line hedges ambition with humor.
claims.alternative: Plans announced in profiles often lapse.
claims.review_trigger: In 2027, check whether he moved (where, and with whom) and whether the dramedy with Hal advanced; update C40, C167 and C122.

claims.claim: Zoe Kazan told Vanity Fair (August 2026) that in his audition he had what she wanted for Cal, 'spikiness, and tenderness, and self-loathing, and canniness', and 'did not audition with a James Dean impression'.
claims.inference: Kazan is describing the Cal she cast, not Zada's personality, so it must never be used as trait evidence. It corroborates his account (C193) that his East of Eden tape was his own take, which contrasts with the Harrelson impression in the Haymitch audition (C198).
claims.alternative: None needed; the claim is limited to what Kazan saw in an audition.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the 2026-10-04 sources add Six-specific markers the record lacked (vigilance welcomed, C192; superstition around a trusted authority's rule, C193; a worry rule internalised from his father, C196; security from a vetted team, C191; mentors credited for guidance, C211), but each is a single phrase in a release-window interview with an ordinary explanation, so together they raise the plausibility of Six without discriminating it from Three or Nine.
claims.inference: The prior record's 'against' noted no worst-case scanning and no visible testing of trust. That remains true. The new markers concern caution and reliance, not testing. He still complies with chosen authorities (Kazan, his father, Lawrence's note per S47) rather than probing them, which fits a Six who has already decided to trust and a deferring Nine equally.
claims.alternative: Media training explains 'careful'. Idiom explains 'safe hands'. Actorly superstition explains 'bad omen'. A father's work ethic explains the motto. Read that way, nothing Six-specific is added.

claims.claim: Interpretation: on the record as of 2026-10-04, Type 3 is now the strongest alternative to Type 6, ahead of Type 9: every fear he names is evaluative (C173, C215); he shaped himself into an impression to win Haymitch (C198); two of his nerve resolutions are result-shaped (C134, C204); collaborators describe his appetite and he describes his own (C26, C131, C200); against it stand his repeated disclaimers of acclaim and approval (C197, C202, C209), his sparse Instagram (C199), and remedies that mostly run through people and preparation rather than results (C171).
claims.inference: Three explains both the fear content and the appetite. Nine explains the calm surface and the tune-outs but not the evaluative fears or the intensity the new sources add (C195, C200, C205, C209). The anti-Three evidence is mostly self-report of the kind interviewers expect.
claims.alternative: Nine still matches the remedy record as closely as Six does (C171), so the ranking of the two alternatives is itself close.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the promotional confound persists. Of the sources opened on 2026-10-04, only the Casting Guild interview (S45) and the GQ awards report (S58) sit outside a release window; S45 is mostly about craft and S58 shows nerves without a stated remedy; no named collaborator describes how he handled a specific pressured moment, and the November 2026 press cycle has not happened.
claims.inference: The last verifier's acceptance test (verify-02) asked for one dated, opened, non-routine discriminator: named or non-promotional testimony on how he handles pressure, a costly choice for trusted people or structure over visibility or ease, or November 2026 press-cycle statements. None of the new items meets it. Harrelson's testimony (C201) is a prediction. The Instagram choice (C199) is not shown to be costly and does not point to Six. 'Safe hands' (C191) is idiomatic press language.
claims.alternative: One could argue the accumulation of small Six-flavoured items across many interviewers amounts to a pattern. But accumulation does not cure a shared confound, because every item comes from the same kind of setting.
claims.review_trigger: After the November 20, 2026 Sunrise release cycle and any non-junket testimony, re-run the verify-02 test and update this claim.

claims.claim: Asked in June 2025 how excited he was to join the Hunger Games universe, he said: 'Insanely excited. Also like really nervous but it's all right, it'll be fine. It's cool. We got like the the best team in the world backing in, an awesome cast.'
claims.inference: S61 at 04:44-04:57. Attributed to Zada by context (only he joined that universe) and a male-range pitch, not by sight. If his, it is a third June 2025 statement in which nerves about the role settle on the strength of the team (with C191 'safe hands' and C212). Listed in C171 as probable only, outside the main tally.
claims.alternative: 'Best team in the world' is franchise boilerplate, and 'it'll be fine' is his habitual quick reassurance (C170). Shubham Maheshwari cannot be excluded by pitch alone.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) Fear content is evaluative throughout, which leans Three: 'embarrass myself' and 'quite insecure... expressing myself' as a teenager (C117, C206), 'terrified I'd be dreadful' (C134), how admired collaborators 'would perceive me' (C13), 'not to be afraid of whether it's good or not' (C76), 'deathly nervous' about idols (C175), public-speaking nerves at the GQ awards (C215) and first-day fear (C217); none concerns losing support or footing (C173). (2) Result-shaped settlers: 'I think it's come out all right' (C134) and 'so nervous for it to come out but I saw it recently and it is fantastic' (C204); probably also reception-based 'ease' (C213, speaker unverified). (3) Performing to win: an impression of Harrelson 'hoping that that was what was going to push me over the line in terms of securing the role' (C198), and the over-delivered tape (C124). (4) Appetite: Lind's 'He just gets what he wants' (C26, C58), Kazan's conditional 'biggest movie star in the world' (C131), 'hungry and obsessive' and 'most vain creatures' (C200), truancy for auditions (C174), a directing goal (C33). (5) Nine material survives: the calm self-presentation (C32, C70, C71, C100, C31, C73), tune-outs tied to nerves (C63, C70, C128), 'day by day' (C203), his father's 'then you let it go' (C196) and a harmony value (C207). (6) Six-specific markers remain thin and idiomatic: no testing of trust or worst-case scanning in practice (C146, C224); the one reliability line once used for Six (Close, C19) is gratitude, not a remedy; the brief's 'security blanket' remark is probably McGregor's (C213) and 'I'm going to smash this' is probably McGregor's too (C212). (7) Nearly every source is release-window press (C44, C226).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3 is now the strongest alternative (C225). It explains the fear content and the appetite with one motive: every fear he names is about being judged or doing badly (C173, C206, C215); he shaped himself into an impression of his predecessor to secure the role (C198) and turned a one-scene request into four scenes with a drone (C124); two of his nerve resolutions run through the result (C134, C204); collaborators and he himself describe hunger, getting what he wants and enjoying watching himself (C26, C58, C131, C200); and his confidence statements are about owning the work ('my own shoes', 'whatever the hell I wanted', C126, C164). Against Three stand his repeated disclaimers of approval and acclaim, including one in the least promotional interview in the record (C197, C202, C209); sparse personal posting during his breakout (C199); crediting luck, ancestors and advocates rather than his own drive (C54, C214); and remedies that run mostly through people and preparation rather than results (C171: 8 against 2). Type 9 is close behind. The remedy record does not separate Six from Nine (C171), and his calm self-presentation and tune-outs (C32, C63, C70, C71, C100, C128, C203) fit it. It is weakened by new self-descriptions of intensity and self-push: 'I'm intense... I keep very much to myself' (C205), 'force myself out of my comfort zone' (C195), 'hungry and obsessive' (C200), 'I can't sidestep these things' (C209), and the self-set opposite-of-Woody challenge (C172). Type 4 was considered because of 'I want to create something that I feel' (C197), solitary intensity (C205) and insecurity about self-expression (C206). It is set aside, not refuted: the evaluative nerves and people-based settling are not specifically Four, and the feeling statements are craft ideals. Type 7 remains set aside as in C169.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: No defensible discriminator exists yet, which is why this record holds. On the current record: (a) Six over Three rests on remedy, where people and structure outnumber results 8 to 2 under C171's stated rule, and on anti-acclaim statements (C197, C202, C209). It is opposed by the fear content (C173) and a clear performing-to-win act (C198). (b) Six over Nine cannot rest on remedy: under C171 structure arranged in advance plus vetted-team security (3) roughly equals tuning out (3 to 4), and the most common category (others' competence, familiarity, company: 5) is shared. It rests only on intensity and self-push items (C195, C200, C205, C209, C172), which are also craft immersion that 9takes's own Butler profile treats as Nine-compatible (S44). (c) The new Six-flavoured markers (vigilance welcomed, C192; an omen around a trusted authority's rule, C193; a worry rule from his father, C196; 'safe hands', C191) are single phrases in release-window press (C224), and none meets the last verifier's test (C226). What would separate the types: what steadies him through the November 20, 2026 Sunrise release and the planned 2027 move, coded under C171's rule (results and reception favour Three; named trusted people and structure arranged in advance favour Six; tuning out or letting the team decide favours Nine); or named testimony from outside the junket format (his coach Miranda Harcourt, a director, his brother) describing what he did under a specific pressure.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Six things this reading does not account for. (1) The appetite collaborators describe and he admits (C26, C58, C131, C200). (2) The impression built to win the role (C198). (3) His recurring confidence about owning the work (C126, C164, C197), which sits beside his fear of admired people. (4) Teenage resistance and truancy (C117, C174, C206), which fit a Nine as well. (5) The planned move away from the place he calls safe, which his reps also want (C40, C218). (6) The Four-compatible artistic self-description (C197, C205). Accounts of his first exchange with Harrelson also conflict (C216), and the baseline hook depends on one of them. A wing is not inferred.
